about: Every real storage array in the public export, itemised: how big, how
many ports, what latency, whether it takes a byte mask, what it does on
a read that collides with a write, how it comes up, and how much of it a
The point of the `technology_mapping` field is to refuse a particular
kind of claim. An array that yosys infers as memory is not a verified
physical RAM, and writing `inferred` where `mapped_and_verified` belongs
would turn an open question into a finished one. Nothing here says
mapped_and_verified, because nothing has been mapped.

arrays.what: the vector register file, flat reference implementation
arrays.read_during_write: read-old: a read in the same cycle as a write to the same register returns the value before the write
arrays.reset_initialisation: none; the contents are undefined until written
arrays.replaceable: whole module, behind its port list
arrays.note: The reference file. A platform would not build this shape: four true read ports and two write ports on one array is not what an SRAM macro gives you, which is why the banked file below exists.

arrays.what: the vector register file, four banks of 1R/1W
arrays.geometry: 4 banks x 32 registers x 16 lanes x 32 bits; bank = phys % 4
arrays.ports_note: per bank. Four banks give four reads per cycle only when the four addresses fall in four different banks; R3 v2's contract is about what happens when they do not.
arrays.reset_initialisation: none; the contents are undefined until written
arrays.replaceable: one bank at a time, behind tnca_rf_bank's port list -- this is the array a platform maps to an SRAM macro

arrays.geometry: per role context; 2 contexts in the shipped configuration
arrays.replaceable: whole module; small enough that flops are the likely mapping

arrays.reset_initialisation: none; a kernel zeroes what it accumulates into

arrays.where: OUTSIDE the export: the platform brings it
arrays.what: the device's data and instruction memory
arrays.geometry: the simulation binding's tnca_mem_model; a platform substitutes its own
arrays.ports_note: plus a combinational instruction-fetch read. The fetch port is separate in the simulation model and a platform is free to arbitrate one port instead, because nothing in the contract requires them to be independent.
arrays.read_latency_cycles: contract: any, >= 0. The core's LSU is tag-matched and tolerates reordering.
arrays.write_latency_cycles: contract: any; a write is answered like a read
arrays.byte_mask_note: 8 byte enables. Sub-word stores rely on it; a memory without byte enables needs a read-modify-write in the adapter.
arrays.read_during_write: the contract does not define a same-cycle collision, because the single port cannot present one
arrays.reset_initialisation: undefined. The host uploads before it launches.
arrays.replaceable: entirely -- this is the adaptation boundary
arrays.evidence: R36-MEM-02 runs a second, independently written model through this boundary

cross_domain.clock: one clock, `clk`, for the whole public top. No domain crossing exists inside it.
cross_domain.reset: one asynchronous-assert reset, `rst_n`, active low. The shell's registers use `always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)`; the core resets synchronously off the same signal.
cross_domain.reset_release: the platform is responsible for releasing rst_n synchronously to clk. The export does not contain a reset synchroniser, and that is a platform responsibility recorded here rather than an omission.
cross_domain.memory_clock: the memory port is synchronous to clk. A memory in another domain needs a synchroniser the export does not provide.
cross_domain.unstated_board_assumptions: none known. Anything a platform must supply is in this object.
